answer: Mount Rainier is located in **Washington** state. The nickname for Washington is **"The Evergreen State."** This nickname was proposed in 1890 by Seattle realtor and historian C.T. Conover to honor the state's abundant evergreen forests. **Mount Rainier** ( _ray-NEER_), also known as **Tahoma** ( _tə-HOH-mə_),[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-11) is a large, active stratovolcano in the Cascade Range of the Pacific Northwest in the United States. The mountain is located in Mount Rainier National Park about 59 miles (95 km) south-southeast of Seattle.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-12) At 14,406 ft[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-15) (4,391 m) it is the highest mountain in the U.S. state of Washington, the most topographically prominent mountain in the contiguous United States,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-NGeo-Bisharat-3) and the tallest in the Cascade Volcanic Arc.

Due to its high probability of an eruption in the near future and proximity to a major urban area, Mount Rainier is considered one of the most dangerous volcanoes in the world, and it is on the Decade Volcano list.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-16) The large amount of glacial ice means that Mount Rainier could produce massive lahars that could threaten the entire Puyallup River valley and other river valleys draining Mount Rainier, including the Carbon, White, Nisqually, and Cowlitz (above Riffe Lake).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-17) According to the United States Geological Survey's 2008 report, "about 80,000 people and their homes are at risk in Mount Rainier's lahar-hazard zones."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-Driedger-18)
Between 1950 and 2022, 471,792 people attempted to climb Mount Rainier according to NPS statistics.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-14_June_2022-19)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-nps-cl_stats-20) Approximately 84 people died in mountaineering accidents on Mount Rainier from 1947 to 2018.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-14_June_2022-19)
Mount Rainier seen from the International Space Station
The many Indigenous peoples who have lived near Mount Rainier for millennia have many names for the mountain in their various languages. A linguistic analysis published in 2025 identified 20 indigenous names for the mountain.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-21)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-22)

Lushootseed speakers have several names for Mount Rainier, including _xʷaq̓ʷ_[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-Tulalip_Place_Names2-7) and _təqʷubəʔ_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-Tulalip_Place_Names2-7)_xʷaq̓ʷ_ means "sky wiper" or "one who touches the sky" in English.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-Tulalip_Place_Names2-7) The word _\_təqʷubəʔ\__ means "snow-covered mountain".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-Tulalip_Place_Names2-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-Bright2-8)_\_təqʷubəʔ\__ has been anglicized in many ways, including "Tacoma" and "Tacobet".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-23)
Cowlitz speakers call the mountain _təx̣ʷúma_ or _təqʷúmen_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-CowlitzDic-9)Sahaptin speakers call the mountain _\_Tax̱úma\__, which is borrowed from Cowlitz.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-Beavert2009-10)
Another anglicized name is Pooskaus.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-24)_[clarification needed_]

# Visit Wilderness
## Why Visit Wilderness?
While wilderness can be appreciated from afar—through online content, television, or books—nothing compares to experiencing it firsthand. Activities like camping, hiking, or hunting allow you to fully enjoy the recreational, ecological, spiritual, and health benefits that wilderness areas offer. These areas provide “outstanding opportunities for solitude or a primitive and unconfined type of recreation,” chances to observe wildlife, moments to renew and refresh, and the physical benefits of outdoor exercise. In many wilderness areas, you can even bring your well-behaved dog.

Mount Rainier Wilderness is located on the west side of the Cascade Range, approximately 50 miles southeast of the Seattle-Tacoma metropolitan area.At 14,410 feet, Mount Rainier itself is the most prominent peak in the Cascade Range. It dominates the landscape of a large part of western Washington State. The mountain stands nearly three miles higher than the lowlands to the west and one and one-half miles higher than the adjacent mountains.Twenty-six named glaciers spill down the slopes, covering approximately 37 square miles, making it the most heavily glaciated peak in the contiguous United States. Mount Rainier is an active volcano that last erupted approximately 150 years ago.
But the distinguishing aspects of this Wilderness only begin with the mountain. Mount Rainier Wilderness is part of a complex ecosystem. Vegetation is diverse, reflecting the varied climatic and environmental conditions encountered across the area's 12,800-feet elevation gradient. Species known or thought to occur in the park include more than 800 vascular plants, 159 birds, 63 mammals, 16 amphibians, 5 reptiles, and 18 native fishes.
The Mount Rainier Wilderness contains 26 named glaciers across 9 major watersheds, with 382 lakes and 470 rivers and streams.

## Location
Mount Rainier National Park is located in Washington State, on the west-side of the Cascade Range, approximately 50 miles southeast of the Seattle-Tacoma metropolitan area. Year-round access to the park is via state route 706 to the Nisqually Entrance in the southwest corner of the park. Limited winter access is available via highway 123 in the southeast corner of the park. The Carbon River/Mowich Lake area, in the northwest corner of the park, is accessed via state route 165 through Wilkeson. In summer only, the north and east sides of the park can be accessed using highway 410.

**Mount Rainier** ( _ray-NEER_), also known as **Tahoma** ( _tə-HOH-mə_),[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-11) is a large, active stratovolcano in the Cascade Range of the Pacific Northwest in the United States. The mountain is located in Mount Rainier National Park about 59 miles (95 km) south-southeast of Seattle.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-12) At 14,406 ft[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-15) (4,391 m) it is the highest mountain in the U.S. state of Washington, the most topographically prominent mountain in the contiguous United States,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-NGeo-Bisharat-3) and the tallest in the Cascade Volcanic Arc.

Due to its high probability of an eruption in the near future and proximity to a major urban area, Mount Rainier is considered one of the most dangerous volcanoes in the world, and it is on the Decade Volcano list.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-16) The large amount of glacial ice means that Mount Rainier could produce massive lahars that could threaten the entire Puyallup River valley and other river valleys draining Mount Rainier, including the Carbon, White, Nisqually, and Cowlitz (above Riffe Lake).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-17) According to the United States Geological Survey's 2008 report, "about 80,000 people and their homes are at risk in Mount Rainier's lahar-hazard zones."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-Driedger-18)
Between 1950 and 2022, 471,792 people attempted to climb Mount Rainier according to NPS statistics.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-14_June_2022-19)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-nps-cl_stats-20) Approximately 84 people died in mountaineering accidents on Mount Rainier from 1947 to 2018.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-14_June_2022-19)
Mount Rainier seen from the International Space Station
The many Indigenous peoples who have lived near Mount Rainier for millennia have many names for the mountain in their various languages. A linguistic analysis published in 2025 identified 20 indigenous names for the mountain.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-21)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-22)

# Visit Wilderness
## Why Visit Wilderness?
While wilderness can be appreciated from afar—through online content, television, or books—nothing compares to experiencing it firsthand. Activities like camping, hiking, or hunting allow you to fully enjoy the recreational, ecological, spiritual, and health benefits that wilderness areas offer. These areas provide “outstanding opportunities for solitude or a primitive and unconfined type of recreation,” chances to observe wildlife, moments to renew and refresh, and the physical benefits of outdoor exercise. In many wilderness areas, you can even bring your well-behaved dog.
Learn more about the diverse ways in which webenefit from wildernessandthreats wilderness areas face today.
1
Mount Rainier Wilderness is located on the west side of the Cascade Range, approximately 50 miles southeast of the Seattle-Tacoma metropolitan area.At 14,410 feet, Mount Rainier itself is the most prominent peak in the Cascade Range. It dominates the landscape of a large part of western Washington State. The mountain stands nearly three miles higher than the lowlands to the west and one and one-half miles higher than the adjacent mountains.Twenty-six named glaciers spill down the slopes, covering approximately 37 square miles, making it the most heavily glaciated peak in the contiguous United States. Mount Rainier is an active volcano that last erupted approximately 150 years ago.
But the distinguishing aspects of this Wilderness only begin with the mountain. Mount Rainier Wilderness is part of a complex ecosystem. Vegetation is diverse, reflecting the varied climatic and environmental conditions encountered across the area's 12,800-feet elevation gradient. Species known or thought to occur in the park include more than 800 vascular plants, 159 birds, 63 mammals, 16 amphibians, 5 reptiles, and 18 native fishes.
The Mount Rainier Wilderness contains 26 named glaciers across 9 major watersheds, with 382 lakes and 470 rivers and streams.

## Location
Mount Rainier National Park is located in Washington State, on the west-side of the Cascade Range, approximately 50 miles southeast of the Seattle-Tacoma metropolitan area. Year-round access to the park is via state route 706 to the Nisqually Entrance in the southwest corner of the park. Limited winter access is available via highway 123 in the southeast corner of the park. The Carbon River/Mowich Lake area, in the northwest corner of the park, is accessed via state route 165 through Wilkeson. In summer only, the north and east sides of the park can be accessed using highway 410.

**Mount Rainier** ( _ray-NEER_), also known as **Tahoma** ( _tə-HOH-mə_),[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-11) is a large, active stratovolcano in the Cascade Range of the Pacific Northwest in the United States. The mountain is located in Mount Rainier National Park about 59 miles (95 km) south-southeast of Seattle.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-12) At 14,406 ft[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-15) (4,391 m) it is the highest mountain in the U.S. state of Washington, the most topographically prominent mountain in the contiguous United States,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-NGeo-Bisharat-3) and the tallest in the Cascade Volcanic Arc.

Due to its high probability of an eruption in the near future and proximity to a major urban area, Mount Rainier is considered one of the most dangerous volcanoes in the world, and it is on the Decade Volcano list.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-16) The large amount of glacial ice means that Mount Rainier could produce massive lahars that could threaten the entire Puyallup River valley and other river valleys draining Mount Rainier, including the Carbon, White, Nisqually, and Cowlitz (above Riffe Lake).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-17) According to the United States Geological Survey's 2008 report, "about 80,000 people and their homes are at risk in Mount Rainier's lahar-hazard zones."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-Driedger-18)
Between 1950 and 2022, 471,792 people attempted to climb Mount Rainier according to NPS statistics.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-14_June_2022-19)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-nps-cl_stats-20) Approximately 84 people died in mountaineering accidents on Mount Rainier from 1947 to 2018.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-14_June_2022-19)
Mount Rainier seen from the International Space Station
The many Indigenous peoples who have lived near Mount Rainier for millennia have many names for the mountain in their various languages. A linguistic analysis published in 2025 identified 20 indigenous names for the mountain.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-21)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-22)

Lushootseed speakers have several names for Mount Rainier, including _xʷaq̓ʷ_[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-Tulalip_Place_Names2-7) and _təqʷubəʔ_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-Tulalip_Place_Names2-7)_xʷaq̓ʷ_ means "sky wiper" or "one who touches the sky" in English.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-Tulalip_Place_Names2-7) The word _\_təqʷubəʔ\__ means "snow-covered mountain".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-Tulalip_Place_Names2-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-Bright2-8)_\_təqʷubəʔ\__ has been anglicized in many ways, including "Tacoma" and "Tacobet".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-23)
Cowlitz speakers call the mountain _təx̣ʷúma_ or _təqʷúmen_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-CowlitzDic-9)Sahaptin speakers call the mountain _\_Tax̱úma\__, which is borrowed from Cowlitz.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-Beavert2009-10)
Another anglicized name is Pooskaus.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier#cite_note-24)_[clarification needed_]

Mount Rainier Wilderness is located on the west side of the Cascade Range, approximately 50 miles southeast of the Seattle-Tacoma metropolitan area.At 14,410 feet, Mount Rainier itself is the most prominent peak in the Cascade Range. It dominates the landscape of a large part of western Washington State. The mountain stands nearly three miles higher than the lowlands to the west and one and one-half miles higher than the adjacent mountains.Twenty-six named glaciers spill down the slopes, covering approximately 37 square miles, making it the most heavily glaciated peak in the contiguous United States. Mount Rainier is an active volcano that last erupted approximately 150 years ago.
But the distinguishing aspects of this Wilderness only begin with the mountain. Mount Rainier Wilderness is part of a complex ecosystem. Vegetation is diverse, reflecting the varied climatic and environmental conditions encountered across the area's 12,800-feet elevation gradient. Species known or thought to occur in the park include more than 800 vascular plants, 159 birds, 63 mammals, 16 amphibians, 5 reptiles, and 18 native fishes.
The Mount Rainier Wilderness contains 26 named glaciers across 9 major watersheds, with 382 lakes and 470 rivers and streams.

## Location
Mount Rainier National Park is located in Washington State, on the west-side of the Cascade Range, approximately 50 miles southeast of the Seattle-Tacoma metropolitan area. Year-round access to the park is via state route 706 to the Nisqually Entrance in the southwest corner of the park. Limited winter access is available via highway 123 in the southeast corner of the park. The Carbon River/Mowich Lake area, in the northwest corner of the park, is accessed via state route 165 through Wilkeson. In summer only, the north and east sides of the park can be accessed using highway 410.

**Washington** is a state in the Pacific Northwest region of the United States. It is commonly referred to as **Washington state**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-5) to distinguish it from the [national capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.");[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-6) both are named after George Washington, a U.S. Founding Father and the first U.S. president. Washington borders the Pacific Ocean to the west, Oregon to the south, and Idaho to the east; it shares an international border with the Canadian province of British Columbia to the north. Olympia is the state capital, and the state's most populous city is Seattle.

Washington is the 18th-largest state, with an area of 71,362 sq mi (184,830 km 2), and the 13th-most populous state, with a population of over 8 million.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-Quick_Facts-2) The majority of Washington's residents live in the Seattle metropolitan area, the center of transportation, business, and industry on Puget Sound,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-8) an inlet of the Pacific Ocean consisting of numerous islands, deep fjords and bays carved out by glaciers. The remainder of the state consists of deep temperate rainforests in the west; mountain ranges in the west, center, northeast, and far southeast, and a semi-arid basin region in the east, center, and south, given over to intensive agriculture. Washington is the second-most populous state on the West Coast and in the Western United States, after California. Mount Rainier, an active stratovolcano, is the state's highest elevation at 14,400 feet (4,389 meters),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-9) and is the most topographically prominent mountain in the [contiguous U.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contiguous_U.S. "Contiguous U.S.")

Four ships of the United States Navy, including two battleships, have been named USS _Washington_ in honor of the state. Previous ships had held that name in honor of George Washington._[citation needed_]

## Symbols, honors, and names
### Unofficial state nickname
[edit]
The state's nickname, "The Evergreen State",[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-Symbols@WA.gov-1)[[310]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-314) was proposed in 1890 by Charles T. Conover of Seattle. The name proved popular as the forests were full of evergreen trees and the abundance of rain keeps the shrubbery and grasses green throughout the year.[[311]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-315) Although the nickname is widely used by the state, appearing on vehicle license plates for instance, it has not been officially adopted.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-Symbols@WA.gov-1) A 2023 bill in the state legislature to formally recognize it as the state nickname was passed by the senate but was returned to committee.[[312]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-316)[[313]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-317)The Evergreen State College, a state-funded institution in Olympia, also takes its name from this nickname.

## Symbols, honors, and names
### Unofficial state nickname
The state song is "Washington, My Home", the state bird is the Willow goldfinch,[[314]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-318) the state fruit is the apple, and the state vegetable is the Walla Walla sweet onion.[[315]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-319) The state dance, adopted in 1979, is the square dance. The state tree is the western hemlock. The state flower is the coast rhododendron. The state fish is the steelhead.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-Symbols@WA.gov-1) The state folk song is "Roll On, Columbia, Roll On" by Woody Guthrie. The unofficial, but popularly accepted, state rock song is "Louie Louie".[[316]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-320)
The state grass is bluebunch wheatgrass. The state insect is the green darner dragonfly. The state gem is petrified wood. The state fossil is the Columbian mammoth. The state marine mammal is the orca. The state soil is Tokul soil.[[317]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-321) The state land mammal is the Olympic marmot.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-Symbols@WA.gov-1) The state seal, featured in the state flag, was inspired by the unfinished portrait of President George Washington by Gilbert Stuart.[[318]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-322) The state sport is pickleball.[[308]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-SR-Pickleball-312)

## Washington State Nickname
### Unofficial Nickname for the State of Washington
Washington was nicknamed "The Evergreen State" by pioneer C.T. Conover (a Seattle realtor and historian) for its abundant evergreen forests. All State Nicknames
Although "The Evergreen State" nickname is very well-known and widely used, it has not been officially adopted by Washington's state legislature.
In 2023 the state senate proposed bill SB 5595 to make the nickname official. In February the senate voted 49-0 to approve. It still needs to be approved by the house and then signed by the governor to become official.

## Symbols, honors, and names
### Unofficial state nickname
[edit]
The state's nickname, "The Evergreen State",[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-Symbols@WA.gov-1)[[310]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-314) was proposed in 1890 by Charles T. Conover of Seattle. The name proved popular as the forests were full of evergreen trees and the abundance of rain keeps the shrubbery and grasses green throughout the year.[[311]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-315) Although the nickname is widely used by the state, appearing on vehicle license plates for instance, it has not been officially adopted.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-Symbols@WA.gov-1) A 2023 bill in the state legislature to formally recognize it as the state nickname was passed by the senate but was returned to committee.[[312]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-316)[[313]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-317)The Evergreen State College, a state-funded institution in Olympia, also takes its name from this nickname.

## Symbols, honors, and names
### Unofficial state nickname
The state song is "Washington, My Home", the state bird is the Willow goldfinch,[[314]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-318) the state fruit is the apple, and the state vegetable is the Walla Walla sweet onion.[[315]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-319) The state dance, adopted in 1979, is the square dance. The state tree is the western hemlock. The state flower is the coast rhododendron. The state fish is the steelhead.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-Symbols@WA.gov-1) The state folk song is "Roll On, Columbia, Roll On" by Woody Guthrie. The unofficial, but popularly accepted, state rock song is "Louie Louie".[[316]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-320)
The state grass is bluebunch wheatgrass. The state insect is the green darner dragonfly. The state gem is petrified wood. The state fossil is the Columbian mammoth. The state marine mammal is the orca. The state soil is Tokul soil.[[317]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-321) The state land mammal is the Olympic marmot.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-Symbols@WA.gov-1) The state seal, featured in the state flag, was inspired by the unfinished portrait of President George Washington by Gilbert Stuart.[[318]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-322) The state sport is pickleball.[[308]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-SR-Pickleball-312)

**Washington** is a state in the Pacific Northwest region of the United States. It is commonly referred to as **Washington state**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-5) to distinguish it from the [national capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.");[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-6) both are named after George Washington, a U.S. Founding Father and the first U.S. president. Washington borders the Pacific Ocean to the west, Oregon to the south, and Idaho to the east; it shares an international border with the Canadian province of British Columbia to the north. Olympia is the state capital, and the state's most populous city is Seattle.

Washington is the 18th-largest state, with an area of 71,362 sq mi (184,830 km 2), and the 13th-most populous state, with a population of over 8 million.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-Quick_Facts-2) The majority of Washington's residents live in the Seattle metropolitan area, the center of transportation, business, and industry on Puget Sound,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-8) an inlet of the Pacific Ocean consisting of numerous islands, deep fjords and bays carved out by glaciers. The remainder of the state consists of deep temperate rainforests in the west; mountain ranges in the west, center, northeast, and far southeast, and a semi-arid basin region in the east, center, and south, given over to intensive agriculture. Washington is the second-most populous state on the West Coast and in the Western United States, after California. Mount Rainier, an active stratovolcano, is the state's highest elevation at 14,400 feet (4,389 meters),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-9) and is the most topographically prominent mountain in the [contiguous U.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contiguous_U.S. "Contiguous U.S.")

## Symbols, honors, and names
### Unofficial state nickname
[edit]
The state's nickname, "The Evergreen State",[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-Symbols@WA.gov-1)[[310]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-314) was proposed in 1890 by Charles T. Conover of Seattle. The name proved popular as the forests were full of evergreen trees and the abundance of rain keeps the shrubbery and grasses green throughout the year.[[311]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-315) Although the nickname is widely used by the state, appearing on vehicle license plates for instance, it has not been officially adopted.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-Symbols@WA.gov-1) A 2023 bill in the state legislature to formally recognize it as the state nickname was passed by the senate but was returned to committee.[[312]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-316)[[313]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state)#cite_note-317)The Evergreen State College, a state-funded institution in Olympia, also takes its name from this nickname.
